passages.title: Lok Baintan Floating Market
text: Lok Baintan is a floating market on the Martapura River in South Kalimantan, about forty-five minutes by boat from the city of Banjarmasin. Unlike ordinary markets, it has no buildings, stalls, or roads. All buying and selling takes place on small wooden boats called jukung.

The market opens very early, usually just after the dawn prayer, and it is busiest between six and eight in the morning. By nine o'clock, most traders have already paddled home. Visitors who want to see it must leave Banjarmasin before sunrise.

Most of the traders are women from villages along the river. They wear wide straw hats called tanggui to protect themselves from the sun, and they paddle their boats skilfully while calling out to buyers. Their boats are piled high with bananas, oranges, vegetables, and freshly made cakes.

One of the most interesting things about Lok Baintan is that some traders still use a barter system. A trader with rice may exchange it for fruit or fish from another boat without using any money. Visitors, of course, pay in cash, and many traders are happy to let tourists take photos.
The market is more than a place to shop. It shows how closely the life of the Banjar people is connected to their rivers, which have been used as roads for hundreds of years.

passages.title: My Internship at a Car Workshop
text: In my second year at SMK, I did a three-month internship at Bengkel Maju Jaya, a car repair workshop in Sidoarjo. I chose this workshop because it was known for its friendly mechanics and its modern equipment.

During the first month, I mostly helped with simple tasks. I changed engine oil, checked tyre pressure, and cleaned spare parts. My supervisor, Pak Agus, always reminded me to put every tool back in its place. At first I thought he was too strict, but later I understood why. One afternoon, a mechanic spent twenty minutes looking for a spanner that someone had left under a car, and the customer had to wait.

In the second month, Pak Agus let me help with brake repairs. I learned how to remove the wheels, check the brake pads, and replace them when they were too thin. Before every car was returned, Pak Agus asked me to test the brakes with him on the road behind the workshop.

The hardest moment came in the third month. A car came in with an engine problem that nobody could find at first. I suggested using the diagnostic scanner I had learned about at school. The scanner showed a fault in one of the sensors, and the problem was fixed in an hour. Pak Agus praised me in front of the other mechanics.
When my internship ended, the owner told me I could apply for a job there after graduation. I left the workshop with more confidence and a clear goal for the future.

passages.title: The Farmer's Clever Daughter
text: Once upon a time, a poor farmer borrowed money from a rich and greedy merchant. When the farmer could not pay it back, the merchant came to his house. The merchant had always wanted to marry the farmer's beautiful and clever daughter, Sari.

"I will make you a deal," said the merchant, standing on the path covered with black and white stones. "I will put one black stone and one white stone into this bag. Sari will take one stone out. If it is white, your debt is forgiven. If it is black, your debt is forgiven too, but Sari must marry me. If she refuses to pick, you will go to prison."

The farmer had no choice. As the merchant bent down to pick up the stones, Sari noticed that he quickly put two black stones into the bag. She realized that whatever she chose, she would have to marry him. If she told everyone he was cheating, he would be embarrassed and angry, and her father might still go to prison.

Sari thought for a moment. Then she put her hand into the bag and took out a stone. Before anyone could see it, she "accidentally" dropped it onto the path, where it was lost among all the other stones.

"Oh, how careless of me!" she said. "But don't worry. We can look at the stone left in the bag. Then we will know which colour I picked." The stone in the bag was, of course, black. So everyone believed Sari had picked the white one. The merchant could not admit that he had cheated. He had to forgive the debt, and he left the house without a word.

passages.title: How to Make a Professional Phone Call at Work
text: Many young workers feel nervous when they have to make phone calls to customers or other companies. These steps will help you sound clear and professional.

Before the call
Write down the purpose of your call and the main points you want to say. Prepare any information you may need, such as an order number or a date. Find a quiet place so the other person can hear you clearly.

Starting the call
Greet the person politely and say your name and the name of your company, for example: "Good morning. This is Dina from Sinar Printing." Then ask if it is a good time to talk.

During the call
Explain the purpose of your call briefly. Speak slowly and clearly, and do not use slang. Listen carefully and write down important information such as names, numbers, and deadlines. If you do not understand something, ask the person to repeat it.

Ending the call
Summarize what you have agreed on, for example: "So, we will deliver the posters on Thursday at ten." Thank the person for their time and say goodbye politely. Wait for the other person to hang up first.

After the call
Send a short email or message to confirm the important details. This helps prevent misunderstandings later.

passages.title: Every School Needs a Garden
text: In many schools, the only plants students see are a few trees in the yard. I believe every school, even one in the middle of a city, should have a garden that students take care of themselves.

First, a school garden is a living classroom. In a garden, students can see how seeds grow, how insects help flowers, and how soil and water affect plants. Lessons in biology, mathematics, and even economics become real when students measure plant growth or calculate the profit from selling vegetables.

Second, gardening encourages healthy eating. Children who grow vegetables are more willing to eat them. A programme in several elementary schools in Bandung found that students who joined gardening activities chose vegetables at lunch twice as often as before.

Third, a garden builds teamwork and responsibility. Plants need water every day, even during holidays. Students must make schedules, share tasks, and solve problems together when pests attack or plants die.

Some people argue that city schools do not have enough land. However, gardens do not need to be large. Vegetables can be grown in pots, on rooftops, or along walls in vertical planters. What is needed is not space, but willingness. Therefore, schools should start small and let students' gardens grow, together with their knowledge.

passages.title: Green Hill Eco-Camp
text: GREEN HILL ECO-CAMP: A WEEKEND AWAY FROM SCREENS

Located 1,200 metres above sea level in the hills of Bogor, Green Hill Eco-Camp offers students and families a chance to enjoy nature while learning how to protect it. The camp is surrounded by pine forest and has a clear river, a vegetable garden, and a small lake where visitors can paddle in wooden canoes.

Programmes. Every group joins three activities: a forest walk with a trained guide, a composting workshop, and a night of storytelling around the campfire. For an extra fee, visitors can also try rope climbing or take a half-day cooking class using vegetables picked from the garden.

Accommodation. Guests may stay in bamboo cabins for up to six people or bring their own tents. All cabins have solar-powered lights, but there is no electricity for charging phones except at the reception building. Hot water is available in the morning and the evening only.

Rules. To keep the camp clean, visitors must take their rubbish to the sorting station and may not bring plastic bottles. A refillable bottle can be borrowed from the reception for free. Fires are allowed only in the campfire area.
Prices start at Rp350,000 per person for a two-day, one-night stay, including meals. Group discounts are available for ten people or more. Please book at least two weeks ahead.

passages.title: Borobudur
text: Borobudur is the largest Buddhist temple in the world. It stands on a hill in Magelang, Central Java, surrounded by green fields and distant mountains. The temple was built around the ninth century, and for hundreds of years it was hidden under volcanic ash and thick forest. It was rediscovered in the early nineteenth century and has been restored several times since then.

Seen from above, Borobudur looks like a giant stone mandala. The temple has nine platforms: six square ones at the bottom and three circular ones at the top. At the very top stands a large central stupa. The walls of the lower levels are covered with thousands of carved panels that tell stories about the life of the Buddha and about everyday life in ancient Java.

On the circular platforms there are many small bell-shaped stupas with holes in them. Inside most of them sits a stone statue of the Buddha. The statues face outward, and their calm faces seem to look over the valley. Visitors who climb to the top at sunrise can see the mist slowly rising from the rice fields, while the sun turns the stone from grey to gold.

Today, Borobudur is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited places in Indonesia. To protect the stone steps from wear, the number of visitors who may climb the temple each day is limited, and visitors are required to wear special sandals.

passages.title: The Lantern Maker's Gift
text: In a small village by the sea, there lived an old lantern maker named Pak Hasan. Every year, before the Harvest Festival, he made hundreds of paper lanterns in bright red, yellow, and blue. Children came from all over the village to watch him work, and he always gave each of them a small lantern to take home.

One year, Pak Hasan fell ill and could not leave his bed. The festival was only a week away, and the villagers were worried. A girl named Sari, who had often watched him work, said, 'I will make the lanterns.' Many people laughed. 'You are only twelve,' they said. 'You cannot do what Pak Hasan does.'

Sari did not listen. She visited Pak Hasan every afternoon, and he taught her from his bed how to bend the bamboo, how to mix the glue, and how to paint the paper. Her first lanterns were crooked, and the colours ran together. Several times she wanted to give up, but she remembered the faces of the children and started again.

On the night of the festival, Sari hung eighty lanterns along the beach. They were not as perfect as Pak Hasan's, but when the candles were lit, the whole shore glowed with warm light. The children cheered, and the villagers stopped laughing. Then Pak Hasan arrived, leaning on a walking stick. He looked at the lanterns for a long time and smiled. 'These are the most beautiful lanterns I have ever seen,' he said, 'because they were made with a brave heart.'

passages.title: How to Make a Simple Rain Gauge
text: A rain gauge measures how much rain falls in a place. You can make a simple one at home with materials that are easy to find.
Materials: a clear plastic bottle, scissors, a ruler, a permanent marker, small stones, and tape.
Steps:
1. Cut the top third off the bottle, just below the place where the bottle starts to narrow.
2. Put some small stones in the bottom of the bottle so that the wind cannot blow it over.
3. Pour water into the bottle until it reaches the top of the stones. This level is your zero line.
4. Using the ruler and the marker, draw a scale in centimetres and millimetres upward from the zero line.
5. Turn the top part you cut off upside down and place it inside the bottle like a funnel. Fasten it with tape.
6. Place the bottle outside in an open area, away from trees and roofs, which can block or drip rain.
7. Read the water level at the same time every day, write the measurement in your notebook, and empty the bottle.

passages.title: Regional Languages Deserve a Place at School
text: Indonesia has more than 700 living languages, but many of them are used by fewer and fewer young people. In several regions, children now speak Indonesian or English at home and hardly understand the language of their grandparents. I believe that regional languages should be taught in schools.

First, language is a carrier of culture. Traditional stories, songs, proverbs, and ceremonies are often told in regional languages, and many of their meanings are lost when they are translated. If a language disappears, a way of understanding the world disappears with it.

Second, learning more than one language is good for the mind. Research suggests that children who grow up using two languages often find it easier to switch between tasks and to learn additional languages later. Therefore, studying a regional language does not hold students back; it can help them.

Some people worry that students are already busy and that English is more useful for their careers. This concern is understandable. However, regional language lessons need only a few hours per week, and they can be combined with arts and local history so that they do not add much extra burden.
In conclusion, schools should give regional languages a regular place in the timetable, so that the next generation can inherit both a modern education and the heritage of their ancestors.
